title: Network Fundamentals and Threats
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain IP addresses, ports, and common protocols, contrast plaintext with encrypted traffic, and recognize spoofing, on-path, and DoS/DDoS attacks.

blocks.text: Every device on a network has an IP address; IPv4 looks like 192.168.1.10 and IPv6 like 2001:db8::1. Services listen on numbered ports: web traffic uses 80 (HTTP) and 443 (HTTPS), secure shell uses 22 (SSH), email transfer uses 25 (SMTP), and domain lookup uses 53 (DNS). A conversation is described by the tuple of source address and port plus destination address and port, carried by TCP (connection-oriented, verified) or UDP (connectionless, fast). You do not need the full OSI model at CC depth, but knowing which protocols speak in plaintext is exam-critical.

The security story in one sentence: anyone who can watch the path can read plaintext protocols in full, while TLS-protected traffic reveals only metadata such as sizes and destination. That contrast is what the module lab shows by capturing your own traffic.

rows: Faking an identity: forged sender, cloned site, forged source address
Authentication, filters, TLS with certificate checks
Attacker sits between you and a service, reading or altering traffic
HTTPS everywhere; avoid unknown networks for sensitive use
A captured valid request is sent again later
Flooding a service or network until it cannot serve
Rate limiting, traffic filtering, absorption services, redundancy

blocks.text: DoS is availability attack number one: one source or a botnet of many (distributed) exhausts bandwidth, connections, or application capacity. Defenses combine filtering upstream, rate limiting, and redundant, scalable infrastructure. Note the asymmetry the exam likes: attack cost scales down with botnets, defense scales up with architecture.

Legacy services, printers, and misconfigured apps still speak plaintext, and attackers who gain a listening position (rogue access point, on-path position) harvest credentials directly. The exam pairs this with segmentation from a later lesson: plaintext protocols belong on isolated networks at minimum, and replaced with TLS-based equivalents wherever possible.

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: Port numbers 80/443/22/25/53 appear constantly; so does the plaintext-versus-TLS distinction. For attack scenarios, name the pattern from its mechanism: faked identity (spoofing), interception (on-path), resend (replay), flood (DoS/DDoS).

blocks.title: Read a connection
steps: Open a terminal and run a connection listing: 'netstat -an' on Windows, or 'ss -tuan' or 'netstat -an' on macOS/Linux.
Find one connection to port 443 and one to port 80 or 53; note the states.
For each, say whether an eavesdropper on the path could read its content, and which protocol carries it.
blocks.expected: Port 443 connections carry HTTPS inside TLS: content unreadable, destination visible. Port 80 HTTP would be fully readable; DNS on 53 is usually plaintext queries, which is why DNS-over-HTTPS exists.

blocks.title: Lab: Inspect HTTP vs HTTPS
blocks.description: Capture your own traffic with Wireshark and compare plaintext HTTP requests with TLS-protected HTTPS sessions. Full guide: labs/inspect-http-vs-https.en.md.

cheatsheet: Ports to memorize: HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, SSH 22, SMTP 25, DNS 53, FTP 20-21.
Plaintext protocols (HTTP, Telnet, FTP, plain DNS) are readable by anyone on the path; TLS protects content.
Spoofing fakes identity; on-path intercepts; replay resends; DoS/DDoS floods availability.
DDoS defense = filtering, rate limiting, absorption, redundancy; never a single magic box.
TCP is connection-verified, UDP is connectionless; both ride on IP addressing.

checkpoint.prompt: A cafe user logs into a website whose address bar shows http:// and the login form submits. What is the direct risk?

choices.A: The site will be rate limited
choices.B: Credentials travel in plaintext and are readable by anyone monitoring the path
choices.C: The browser will refuse to send the form
choices.D: DNS poisoning of the cafe router

checkpoint.explanation: HTTP is unencrypted, so the username and password cross the network in the clear, visible to an on-path observer such as a rogue access point operator. The browser sends it anyway; DNS poisoning is a different attack.

checkpoint.prompt: An online store is unreachable worldwide; traffic analysis shows millions of requests from distributed sources. Which attack and which CIA element?
checkpoint.explanation: Distributed flooding that makes the service unreachable is a DDoS attack, and its target is availability. No data is read, altered, or disputed in this scenario.
